title: Lazarus raised; tears and cry (John 11:4–44)
english: the illness is not toward death. Raising Lazarus from sickness was not of such glory and wonder as raising him from the dead.
For this reason he stayed, that Lazarus might die and be buried and the Jews might not say he raised one who had only swooned.
For this reason he foretells, lest when he suddenly goes there they be troubled.

"They are seeking to stone you" and what follows they said as not yet perfected and thinking that he also suffered unwillingly, so that he said this: "Are there not twelve hours" and what follows (John 11:9).

Just as the day is unstable, shifting from hour to hour, so also is human opinion—that is, the Jews'. If the one who walks in day does not stumble, how would I who enlighten all undergo the things of the ill-advised?
He speaks as to one living when he says "let us go"; for to him Lazarus lived as God.
Lest we appear without affection, let us hasten to our friend's salvation, overlooking Jewish plots.
The Lord called himself life, not a living being; for a living being is receptive of life, but life is what supplies living, as wisdom and the wise: the one receives, the other gives.
If this had not happened by God's economy, the evangelist would not have mentioned it; it happened so that even unwilling they might come and witness the sign.

Christ, grieved and seeing grief moved in himself and the flesh nodding toward tears, rebukes the flesh by the Holy Spirit's power, which, not bearing the movement of the Godhead united to it, trembles and masters the grief; for it was not fitting for the one who brings the hope of resurrection to weep over a dead man.
As one without love of display he said this and pretends not to know, because of the lowliness of human nature—he who knows all as God—that he might draw many to the place.
He asks not as ignorant, he who knew this from a long distance, but so that on the pretext of pointing out the place they may come and see the sign.
Sympathizing with those who wept, he wept—not for the one he was about to raise.
Again he rebukes the passion, that we may learn that he became man without change as we are.
Because of the excess of the wonder Martha somehow again disbelieves.
In things beyond nature God's glory appears. Because of the hearers' weakness he says the Father's glory; because of freedom from vanity he did not say "you will see my glory" but the Father's.
Being equal to the Father he thanks him, that we may give thanks to the one above ourselves. This is said among friends and equals.

As if the soul were far off he calls with a cry, not as if it were in the tomb, as the Greeks' children mythologize. The Lord's cry was a type of the "great trumpet" that will sound in the common resurrection. The command is God-befitting and royal.

title: Council; Caiaphas; withdrawal (John 11:44–55)
english: resurrection: that with hands and feet and eyes bound he came out walking. By the loosing they witnessed that it was not a phantom but Lazarus.

From this it is clear that not all the Jews around Mary saw Lazarus's resurrection, but some of them, who also believed in Christ. The rest, hearing from those who had seen, went down to the Pharisees, stirring them against him as one who had dared something unholy; for they accused him as having ordered the buried to be dug up. Then he says they gathered a council against him and reasoned, saying: If we leave him thus, all will believe in him and the Romans will come upon us on suspicion of tyranny and will destroy our city. These things, even if they said them from envy, also came out when they did not expect it, when they crucified him.
They accused him as having dared something unholy—as ordering the buried to turn back. After so many proofs they spoke as of a bare man, not knowing that he was the Christ, maker of the signs.

If, they say, those who believe in him make him king, the Romans will come upon us as having tyrannized and will strip us of everything. To avoid undergoing the terrible things they said he should be destroyed. And when they murdered him, the grievous things came out against them.
When priesthoods became purchasable, priests no longer served for their whole lifetime nor by lineage, but the Romans gave it to whom they wished, succeeding them when they wished.

With a mouth speaking only, not with the Holy Spirit's grace touching his heart, the gift of foretelling was given him for the honor of the priesthood, not as to a prophet. Prophesying benefits no one. It fits against those who do not believe rightly yet foretell some things, who if they say on the day of judgment to the Lord, "Lord, did we not prophesy in your name," will hear that "I never knew you" (Matthew 7:22–23). So one must not be led astray from this; for prophecy is not a fruit of good works by which we recognize the saints, but wholly the Spirit's work, even if it speaks through human instruments—that is, human tongues.
Christ underwent death for the common salvation of all.

The evangelist calls children of God the faithful from the nations who were "far" and have become "near" into "one body," having Christ as one head (Ephesians 2:13–16). He proclaims beforehand what he does not know, glorifying Christ by necessity as also Balaam did.

He withdraws for the Jews' condemnation, not from cowardice, and teaches us at the peak of anger not to throw ourselves into dangers. He fled waiting for the fitting time of the passion and sparing their salvation.
Those who had sinned voluntary or involuntary faults did not keep the Passover unless they had been purified

title: Bethany anointing; palms; nations' colt (John 12:1–16)
english: with the customary purification.
But Lazarus did not die at once after appearing; he lived on eating and drinking and doing the usual things, which the evangelist said as marveling.

Martha is seen as practical virtue, Mary as spiritual contemplation. Others take Martha as the old covenant, which prepares the Lord's table through the testimony of the old things, established by doctrines concerning Christ, and Mary as evangelical instruction, which anointing the Lord's feet with myrrh—that is, his economy upon the earth—filled the whole earth with fragrance, which is the house of all humanity. Others understand Martha as the Jews' synagogue wanting to serve God through fleshly things, and Mary as the church from the nations offering spiritual sacrifices and fragrant faith to God and wiping the blessing from his flesh through mystical participation.
For in the rank of fragrance the knowledge of Christ was going to fill the world.
Judas blames that she brought myrrh and not silver, not knowing what is truly good; for the gift-bearing toward God ought to be preferred to the poor.
The Lord endured him stealing, lest he say that for love of money and want I made the betrayal. Judas was a temple robber, stealing money dedicated to God.

Toward conviction of the senseless Judas he mentioned the burial. What he means is this: wait a little and I will go away. He speaks in defense of the woman, lest he seem to prefer himself to the poor.

Saying "leave her" he convicts Judas's hypocrisy as blaming things worthy of praise. And since the myrrh's expense was not for luxury but for mystical need, he apologizes for Mary, even if she did not know the economy of the mystery. And by mentioning burial he shames Judas, that for shameful gain he was going to betray the teacher.
When there is need of spiritual liturgy or hymnody, one must not leave these and go off about beneficence, but after these liturgies.
They almost made a charge against the man because he had suffered well.
As to one who had conquered death they met him with palms; for David's prophecy is fulfilled through this.

The donkey is a type of the nations, whom the Lord, being unclean, made subject. The colt is a type of the nations, whom the Lord, sitting, leads up into the "Jerusalem above," of which the earthly is a type. He calls them a colt because they were untrained in the faith according to piety.
For this reason they did not know, lest they take offense if, being king, he is going to suffer such things, and because they could not at once contain the knowledge of the kingdom.
